title: Section A practice questions and mark scheme points
subject: English Language
source: Seeded from english-language/y11 lessons 47, 48 (Section A practice questions and mark scheme points (pupil PDF))
intro: Answer every question. Show your working. Mark it with the mark scheme and log any errors in your repair list.

questions.q: in the portal response box, answer Q3. Starter: 'The writer presents walking as...'
questions.a: Mark scheme points: list of sensory details ('bakery', 'coffee', 'wet dogs') shows noticing; metaphor 'slowness... a kind of wealth'; contrast of traffic anger with clear head; structure from past (car) to present (walking) to direct appeal; final line 'the journey was the point' as a reflective ending. Top answers weave language and structure with effects.
questions.model: Model opening shared after: 'The writer presents walking as a gift of time. The metaphor "slowness turns out to be a kind of wealth" reverses our usual idea that speed is valuable; structurally, the column moves from the angry past ("shouting at strangers through glass") to a calm present, so the reader feels the change.'

questions.q: Self-mark Q3 with the mark scheme points; add one missing point.
write the structural point you missed in one sentence.
questions.a: For example: The final direct appeal turns a personal story into advice for the reader.
Q1: they spent forty minutes a day in traffic (or were shouting at strangers through glass). Q2: thirty-five minutes.
questions.model: Underline 'paragraph 1' and 'reason'. Scan, find 'forty minutes a day in traffic', write it in a few words. Q2: scan for 'good weather': thirty-five minutes.

questions.q: In the time plan, Section A gets about...
Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: About 1.8 minutes a mark: so a 1-mark question gets under two minutes.

questions.q: Q6 in the portal response box. Starter: 'The writer presents the city at night as...'
questions.a: Mark scheme points: personification ('every doorway seems to hold its breath', 'the river breathes'); 'sickly yellow patience'; metaphor 'a different nation'; humour ('as gravely as a bishop'); structure: from the secret, through discomfort ('I do not pretend'), to the lesson and direct appeal.
questions.model: Model opening shared after: 'The writer presents the city at night as a strange, living place. Personification in "every doorway seems to hold its breath" makes the streets feel watchful and tense; structurally, the honest turn "I do not pretend the walk was wholly pleasant" makes her final advice more trustworthy.'

questions.q: Q7 in the portal response box. Starter: 'Both writers present walking as...'
questions.a: Mark scheme points: both say walking clears the mind ('my head is clear' / 'a mind scrubbed clean'); both notice small details of their city; both end with a direct appeal; differences: daily routine versus a midnight adventure; modern column versus private letter; noticing places versus noticing people; tone light and reflective versus vivid and slightly comic.

questions.q: Self-check: did every Q7 paragraph mention both texts?

questions.a: Q4: midnight. Q5 any two: gas-lamps; fog over the bridges; a coffee-stall with three cab-men; a watchman; milk-carts (on her return).
questions.model: Q4: scan for a time: 'at midnight'. Q5: two separate details on two lines: 'a coffee-stall with cab-men'; 'a watchman'.
